title: Additive-noise rigidity, a sharp growth threshold and an exact nonlinear-mixture boundary for Gaussian kernel spaces
shortTitle: No noise rescues nonlinear drift in a Gaussian kernel space, but mixtures of Gaussian branches can
oneLine: Any additive noise forces affine drift; mixtures of Gaussian branches pass exactly when their gates grow slowly enough in the complex plane: probit gates up to a threshold, logistic gates never
abstract: Kernel methods such as kernel EDMD learn how a random system evolves by averaging smooth test functions over one random step, and their analysis often assumes that this averaging keeps a Gaussian kernel space (RKHS) invariant. An earlier Evidence Press release showed that a step X' = F(x) + Z keeps the space only if F is affine, but only for noise whose characteristic function has a Gaussian lower bound, and asked whether that hypothesis can be dropped and whether any state-dependent non-Gaussian transition can be admissible. This candidate proves three results. (A) For every noise law, boundedness between global Gaussian RKHSs forces F to be injective and affine, with an exact operator-norm formula; the noise enters only through a deterministic composition. (B) More generally, composition from a stationary source whose spectral measure dominates Lebesgue measure near zero into a Hilbert space of entire functions forces an affine map whenever the target's evaluation norms have zero exponential type in the imaginary direction; for every positive type a nonlinear map such as x + c·sin x can be bounded, so this growth condition is sharp. (C) A finite state-dependent mixture of Gaussian branches with a common linear part and fixed covariances is bounded exactly when each mixing probability extends to an entire function within an explicit quadratic growth budget, so nonlinear conditional means are admissible. With branch variance q, a Gaussian-bump gate e^(−αx²) is admissible exactly when α ≤ 8q/(1+4q), a probit gate Φ(βx) exactly when β² ≤ 16q/(1+4q), and a logistic gate never. The same Gram-matrix argument gives a several-variable no-cancellation theorem for sums of weighted composition operators on Fock spaces with a common invertible linear part; the one-variable case was obtained concurrently and more generally by Cho, Choe, Koo and Tien and by Lin, Lu, Yang and Zu. Limits: global RKHS norms only, not finite-data accuracy or other norms; the noise is formal at the operator level. AI-assisted, unrefereed candidate; no external peer review, independent reproduction or formal verification is claimed.
citeText: Anonymous (2026). Additive-noise rigidity, a sharp growth threshold and an exact nonlinear-mixture boundary for Gaussian kernel spaces. Version 0.1.0-candidate. Evidence Press. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24550034
evidence: A 21-page paper with a context-first introduction, written proofs of all theorems, limits, open problems and an AI-use statement. Three Python programs accompany it: code/verify.py runs 97 checks (spectral constants, tube norm, exact scalar thresholds, Gram identities against direct quadrature, triangular-noise norms, the warping identity and smoothing formulas; numpy 2.3.5, scipy 1.17.0, sympy 1.14.0) and code/check_extensions.py runs 63 checks, almost all in 50-digit mpmath arithmetic (the threshold a_*, growth bounds, the probit bound and threshold, the logistic pole, a two-variable Fock Gram matrix, the threshold identities); every check raises an error on failure, even under python -O. code/make_figures.py draws the phase diagram. These finite calculations test constants and implementations; they do not certify the analytic theorems. A clean replay in optimised mode reproduced the recorded results; changing the probit threshold from 4D to 2D makes six checks fail. Linux CI reruns all three programs and compares outputs exactly except scipy's own quadrature error estimate, compared within a declared relative tolerance of 1e-4.

keyResults: Theorem 2.1 (proof): for every probability law of the noise Z, the transition X' = F(x) + Z maps one global Gaussian RKHS boundedly into another only if F is injective and affine; the operator norm has an exact formula. This removes the characteristic-function hypothesis of the predecessor release.

Theorem 3.1, Proposition 3.2 and Corollary 3.3 (proof): composition from a stationary source whose spectral measure dominates Lebesgue measure near zero into a Hilbert space of entire functions forces an affine map when the target's evaluation norms have zero exponential type in the imaginary direction; for every positive type a bounded nonlinear example exists, so the condition is sharp.

Theorems 5.1 and 5.5 (proof): a finite mixture of Gaussian branches with a common linear part and fixed, possibly different, covariances is bounded exactly when each mixing probability extends to an entire function within an explicit quadratic growth budget.

Corollaries 6.1 and 6.2 (proof): with branch variance q, a Gaussian-bump gate e^(−αx²) is admissible exactly when α ≤ 8q/(1+4q) (q = 1/12, 1/4, 3/4 at α = 1/2, 1, 3/2); a probit gate Φ(βx) exactly when β² ≤ 16q/(1+4q); a logistic gate never.

Corollary 5.3 (proof): on Fock spaces in several variables, a finite sum of weighted composition operators with a common invertible linear part and distinct shifts is bounded exactly when every summand is bounded.

Credit and limits: the norm formula, multiplier criterion and smoothing spectrum are classical; the one-variable Fock no-cancellation statement is due concurrently, and more generally, to Cho, Choe, Koo and Tien and to Lin, Lu, Yang and Zu. Global RKHS norms only; branches with different linear parts, state-dependent covariances and general Markov transitions remain open.

decisionObject.description: Decide which random transition models can keep a Gaussian kernel space (RKHS) invariant: whether any additive noise rescues nonlinear drift, how sharp that rigidity is, and which state-dependent Gaussian mixtures are admissible.
decisionObject.scope: Global Gaussian RKHS norms; additive noise of any law; stationary sources into Hilbert spaces of entire functions; finite Gaussian mixtures with a common linear part and fixed covariances; Fock-space sums with a common invertible linear part.
